title: Elucidating the Mechanisms and Relevance of Cocaine-Induced Plasticity of Inhibitory G Protein Signaling in the Prelimbic Cortex
text:
Despite the prevalence and adverse consequences of psychostimulant use disorders, there are no FDA-
approved interventions for their treatment. Recent work has shown that repeated cocaine exposure in mice
weakens an inhibitory signaling pathway in the prefrontal cortex and that this adaptation is sufficient to provoke
an array of cellular and behavioral hallmarks of addiction. The proposed research seeks to define the cellular
and neurochemical mechanisms underlying this neuroadaptation and to evaluate the therapeutic potential of
strengthening this inhibitory signaling pathway to reverse the consequences of repeated cocaine exposure.

title: Glycoengineering of antibodies to modulate immune functions
text:
Antibodies are an important class of therapeutic glycoproteins, in which the Fc domain
glycosylation plays an essential role in dictating antibody's functions. The proposed research
aims to develop efficient enzymatic and chemoenzymatic methods for producing
glycoengineered antibodies and novel antibody-drug conjugates with enhanced efficacy for the
treatment of human diseases.

title: Leveraging PfCRT Structure to Discern Function and Predict Emergence of Drug-Resistant Malaria
text:
Drug resistance in Plasmodium falciparum, the deadliest of the malaria parasites, is associated with genetic
variations in the chloroquine resistance transporter (PfCRT). This project integrates structural, functional,
computational, imaging, and in vitro gene-editing approaches to decipher at a molecular level how PfCRT works
and evolves to balance its physiological function and its role in effluxing first-line 4-aminoquinoline drugs. Our
combinatorial approach is designed to characterize and predict emerging drug resistance and inform the
selection of efficacious antimalarial therapies.

title: Creating protease-responsive hydrogels to generate cell-specific niches within matrices
text:
Human tissues comprise diverse cell populations with distinct matrix requirements for optimal function,
creating a fundamental challenge in designing hydrogel scaﬀolds. We propose developing innovative
materials where speciﬁc cell types can dynamically modify their local microenvironment to promote targeted
processes like angiogenesis or osteogenesis within a single hydrogel scaﬀold. This biomimetic approach will
signiﬁcantly advance our ability to recreate the complex hierarchical organization of native tissues, providing
both improved regenerative medicine outcomes and a powerful platform for studying cell-matrix interactions
in development and disease.

title: Mechanisms of Central Synaptic Dysfunction in SMA
text:
Neuronal control of movement is extensively studied not only because it underlies fundamental human behaviors
but also because neurodegenerative diseases that affect the motor system represent a significant burden for
human health. We have identified abnormalities in the way neurons communicated with each other by means of
abnormal removal of synaptic connections, which result in pathological situations. Additionally, we will be
investigating the cellular and neuronal circuit mechanisms involved in postural and locomotor deficits since this
proposal describes a multidisciplinary effort aimed to determine the molecular and cellular mechanisms that may
contribute to human diseases such as spinal muscular atrophy—the leading genetic cause of death in infancy.

title: Understanding and targeting molecular and cellular events responsible for pulmonary arteriovenous malformation development, growth and regression
text:
Understanding which endothelial subpopulations and signaling pathways are responsible for the development of
pulmonary arteriovenous malformations (PAVM) will help us develop medical therapies to prevent, arrest and
potentially regress PAVMs.
We will test two repurposed drugs, Tacrolimus (FK506) and Enzastaurin, as well as novel drugs predicted in
silico (ie Brivanib) in our novel mouse model of PAVM in vivo as well as in in vitro in induced pluripotent stem
cell derived endothelial cells (iPSC-ECs) as well as organ cultures from HHT patients.
Given that these three drugs are ready to be tested in clinical trials, our research is in line with the NIH’s mission
to increase knowledge and enhance health, lengthen life, reduce illness and disability by applying fundamental
knowledge to diseases without a cure.

title: Enteroid Core
text: ENTEROID CORE – Project Summary The Enteroid Core (EC) is a multi-service resource that provides Program Project and Core Investigators and their laboratories the tools and advice needed to establish and utilize human intestinal stem cell-derived enteroids/colonoids for understanding the pathogenesis of enteric bacterial infections. The Enteroid Core provides established enteroid and colonoid cultures from JHU biobank, expertise and training in the use of human small intestinal and colonic enteroid monolayers, growth factor-conditioned media required for propagation, maintenance, and differentiation of enteroid cultures, including M cells, as well as assistance in troubleshooting growth, differentiation, and use of enteroids for study of host-pathogen interactions in each project. The Enteroid Core works in close collaboration with the Immunology Core to develop novel co-culture models of human enteroids/colonoids with primary human innate immune cells. Our collaborative work during the current award period resulted in the first human immune-enteroid co-culture model that included monocyte-derived macrophages. In addition, the Enteroid Core developed techniques and protocols to assist Project laboratories achieve their proposed Aims including lentiviral transduction of human enteroids/colonoids for stable knockdown (via shRNA) of target genes (e.g. MUC2 for Project 1 (EAEC); MRP5 for Project 3 (ETEC)) and differentiation of specialized intestinal epithelial cell types (e.g. M cells for Project 2 (Shigella)). This renewal application seeks to continue these collaborative efforts to provide Projects 2 (Shigella) and 3 (ETEC) and the Immunology Core with media necessary for propagating human enteroids/colonoids and growing them as monolayers as well as media to normally differentiate enteroids/colonoids as well as to express M cells (Project 2 (Shigella)). Project 1 (EAEC) investigators have been trained to make conditioned media independently and will receive quality control support from the EC. The EC will continue to help with troubleshooting problems with culturing enteroids as well as use of enteroids for each project. In collaboration with the Immunology Core, the EC will continue developing innate immune cell-enteroid co-culture models to include human monocyte-derived dendritic cells and intraepithelial lymphocytes. In addition to new co-culture models, the EC and Immunology Core will increase the complexity of co-cultures through increased direct physical interaction of enteroid monolayers with immune cells normally present in the lamina propria, using commercially available 3D cell culture scaffolds, perfusion systems, and recently developed anaerobic chamber used for human enteroid monolayers.

title: Prediction and Significance of Cancer in Idiopathic Inflammatory Myositis
text:
While it is established that a subgroup of patients with idiopathic inflammatory myopathies (IIM) are diagnosed
with contemporaneous cancer, the ability to predict cancer at the patient-level is imperfect. This proposal will
develop and externally validate the first predictive tool to determine cancer risk and guide clinical decision-
making in IIM patients (Aim 1). In Aim 2, the relationship between cancer emergence, cancer elimination, and
IIM outcomes will be determined using novel liquid biopsy cancer detection technologies, providing insights
into novel IIM treatment strategies and improvements in disease monitoring.

title: Consequences of retrotransposition on genome integrity
text:
This project will investigate the roles of DNA-damaging transposons during tumorigenesis, including their
contributions to the progression of Barrett's esophagus to esophageal cancer. Using in vitro experimental
systems and new approaches to genomic analyses in human tissues, we will determine the full scope of DNA
rearrangements attributable to transposon activity.

title: Opportunistic Atherosclerotic Cardiovascular Disease Risk Estimation at Abdominal CTs with Robust and Unbiased Deep Learning
text:
We seek to develop new deep learning algorithms to utilize already-acquired abdominal computed tomography
scans and pair them with a patient’s electronic medical records to predict the risk of future cardiovascular
disease. Unlike traditional risk prediction techniques, our proposed tools utilize quantitative imaging measures
of multiple tissues related to cardiovascular health as well as a patient’s prior clinical history. If successful, our
algorithms could be used to explain a patient’s risk status to their clinician and ultimately, could be used to screen
and intervene in millions of patients who are unaware of their risk for heart disease.

title: Linking Mitochondrial Calcium to Histone Methylation Underlying Lung Regeneration
text:
Chronic Respiratory Diseases, such as Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD), are the third leading
cause of death and disability in the United States, generating $50 billion dollars in expenses every year. There
are no cures for this disease group. We want to study lung healing so that we can develop new treatments to
help people with Chronic Respiratory Diseases.

title: Whole genome sequencing of Escherichia coli and Salmonella enterica isolates screened from companion and food animals with potential public and animal health importance
text:
One hundred E. coli and one hundred Salmonella enterica isolates with potential human and animal
health importance will be selected and subjected to whole genome sequencing. Shiga toxin-producing E. coli
(STEC), enterotoxigenic E. coli (ETEC), enteropathogenic E. coli (EPEC), and more prevalent Salmonella
serotypes will be preferentially selected. At least 90 assembled high-quality complete genomes or draft
genomes from each bacterial species will be submitted to NCBI GenBank and made publicly accessible.

title: MOLECULAR MECHANISMS OF NEUROPROTECTION IN POLYGLUTAMINE-DEPENDENT DEGENERATION
text:
Age-dependent neurodegeneration is a major health and socioeconomic burden that will worsen as
 human lifespan steadily increases. The mechanisms of degeneration initiation and progression, as well
as protective pathways to combat disease, remain poorly understood. We propose to elucidate how proteins
implicated in the polyglutamine family of degenerative diseases are regulated in intact animals and in human
cells with the purpose of learning new ways to combat them therapeutically.

title: Genetic Characterization and Exploration of Mu-Opioid Receptor Signaling in C. elegans
text:
While opioids are the most effective pharmacological treatment for pain, opioids have harmful side effects
including tolerance and severe abuse liability that affect millions of Americans. This proposal aims to identify and
characterize genetic regulators of opioid drug action and has the potential to reveal targets for modulating
existing opioids to reduce harmful side effects.

title: INHIBITION OF EZH2 TO ENHANCE ADOPTIVE T-CELL THERAPIES FOR CANCER
text:
This proposal seeks to enhance the potency of adoptive T-cell immunotherapies including chimeric antigen
receptor (CAR) T-cells against cancer by studying the role of EZH2 in tumor cells, the tumor microenvironment,
and CART/T-cells. The proposed research is highly relevant to public health because T-cell immunotherapies
still fail in a significant subset of patients despite being used routinely in clinical practice. The initiative follows
the NCI's mission to improve the treatment of cancer, advance scientific knowledge, and help patients 
 live
longerhealthier lives.

title: Coevolution and Functional Interactions in the Non-Coding Genome
text:
The aim of this research proposal is to gain mechanistic understanding of the relationships among genomic
variation, phenotype, and disease. The proposed research will combine data from DNA-DNA proximity ligation
assays and multiple genome alignments to extract coevolutionary information about DNA elements and to infer
the network of functional interactions among them. The PI has already made important contributions to the field
of 3D genomics employing similar approaches.

title: Improving muscle quality and enhancing shoulder function following rotator cuff injury through blood flow restriction therapy
text:
Rotator cuff injuries have an increasing impact on our Veteran patients as they age. The incorporation of
innovative interventions, such as blood flow restriction therapy, becomes crucial in addressing the unique
rehabilitation needs of elderly Veterans, offering potential benefits in pain management and functional
recovery. This preclinical study holds strong relevance to the well-being of our VA patients as it serves as a
crucial intermediary step, providing essential insights and validating the potential clinical translation of blood
flow restriction therapy for patients.

title: Harnessing Androgen-Driven Immune Modulation to Enhance Immunotherapy for Endocrine Cancers
text:
Immunotherapy has revolutionized cancer treatment, but endocrine tumors such as adrenal, ovarian, and
breast cancers often fail to respond due to poor immune infiltration. This research investigates the novel role of
androgens in enhancing anti-tumor immunity, transforming “cold” tumors into “hot” ones, and sensitizing them
to immune checkpoint blockade (ICB). By elucidating the mechanisms of androgen-mediated immune
activation and testing combined hormonal therapy and ICB, this work has the potential to improve
immunotherapy outcomes for patients with endocrine cancers, ultimately reducing disease burden and
enhancing survival.

title: Mucosally active biomaterial immunomodulators for chronic rhinosinusitis
text:
Chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps (CRSwNP) affects a substantial portion of the United States
population, but existing treatments for it are only partially effective, and recurrence rates are high. This project
develops self-assembling peptide nanomaterials that can be delivered to nasal passages and that stimulate
the production of antibodies that neutralize one of the key drivers of CRSwNP, thymic stromal lymphopoietin
(TSLP). In mouse models of CRSwNP, this technology will be developed and optimized, opening the door not
only for a novel treatment for CRSwNP but for inflammatory diseases of mucosal tissues broadly.

title: Characterizing the role of LDL related receptor 1 (Lrp1) as host entry factor for multiple bunyaviruses
text:
Arthropod-transmitted viruses belonging to the large Bunyavirales order (such as Oropouche virus (OROV), La 
Crosse virus (LACV), and Rift Valley fever virus (RVFV)) can cause significant disease outbreaks in humans
throughout the world. Our proposed work will define critical host factors for virus entry and identify novel targets 
that will facilitate pan-bunyavirus therapeutic development. Recent outbreaks and the emerging nature of 
bunyaviruses, coupled with a rising potential of misuse in the form of bioterrorism, underscore the importance of 
the proposed studies to global health.
